name: Vocabulary Richness
description: Analyzes the lexical opulence of a text by measuring how effectively vocabulary expands relative to the text's length. While basic Type-Token Ratio (TTR) severely punishes longer texts, this algorithm utilizes Root TTR (Guiraud's Index) and Yule's Characteristic K to evaluate 'richness' independent of document size. Large Language Models (LLMs) operate under strict probability parameters that heavily penalize the use of obscure, highly specific, or low-probability words. As a result, AI-generated text quickly reaches a 'vocabulary plateau'—a point where it stops introducing novel words and begins endlessly looping its safe, high-probability core dictionary. Human writers, however, possess a much higher threshold for lexical fatigue, continuously introducing fresh, context-specific, and unpredictable words no matter how long the text becomes.
algorithm: Guiraud's Root TTR & Yule's K Characteristic
mechanism: The scanner maps the total number of words (tokens) against the number of unique words (types). Instead of a simple division, it calculates the Root TTR (Types / √Tokens), forcing a curve that levels the playing field for longer documents. It simultaneously calculates Yule's K to measure the statistical probability of a randomly drawn word being a repetition of a previously used word. If the Root TTR score is unnaturally low and Yule's K indicates severe, mathematically smooth repetition—meaning the author gave up on finding unique vocabulary far too early—it is a critical indicator of an LLM's probability-constrained text generation.
useCase: Highly effective for auditing long-form content such as whitepapers, eBooks, extended essays, and academic literature. It exposes AI models that can mimic human eloquence for a few paragraphs but fail to sustain human-level vocabulary expansion over thousands of words.
strengths:
• Exceptional at detecting AI in long-form generation, as the lexical deficit of LLMs becomes more mathematically obvious the longer the text runs.
• Root TTR and Yule's K natively correct for document length, making this metric highly stable and robust across vastly different text sizes.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives in rigid technical writing (e.g., software documentation, medical reports) where the explicit repetition of exact terminology is mandatory and synonyms are prohibited.
• Ineffective on micro-texts (like tweets or short product descriptions) because the text ends before the 'vocabulary plateau' can be statistically proven.
parameters:
Analysis: Lexical Expansion Rate & Repetition Probability
Metrics: Guiraud's Index (Root TTR) & Yule's Characteristic K
Output: 0-100 Lexical Plateau and Poverty Score
accuracy: Moderate to High — 76-85% accuracy on extended texts. It is a highly reliable foundational metric in computational stylometry. AI models currently cannot optimize for human-level Root TTR without hallucinating or breaking semantic coherence.

references.title: Yule, G. U. (1944). The Statistical Study of Literary Vocabulary. Cambridge University Press.
Uchendu, A. et al. (2020). Authorship Attribution for Neural Text Generation. EMNLP.
